Daniel is a neutral party who can point out a problem on his way out the door entirely uninvested in what happens next.

segments.text: I think there's one more reason so many people split up after watching Jigsaw, maybe the most important factor in all this. I first heard about Jigsaw when it came out in 2018. At the time, I was in a relationship with someone who was pretty clearly not a good match for me long-term. And so when I heard how many couples this special was breaking up, I thought, no way am I watching that. I know it'll happen. My relationship will never survive this.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I'm not in that situation anymore. So recently, I decided it was finally safe to see the show. And I have to say, I was totally right to be scared of it. There are moments in there that I know would have gotten me back then, like this terrible thought about being in a relationship that you don't know how to leave--

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: But you just sit there, and you wait. You wait looking for an excuse to get out, just waiting for them to do something unforgivable so that you can actually break up with them with a real excuse and leave with your head held high. But because unlike you, they're not a piece of shit, they won't do that.

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: So you have to start lowering your standards for what unforgivable is.

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: One week in, you're like, if they cheat on me, this is perfect. I can leave with my head held high, and I will not look like a dick. Nine weeks later, they're faithful, and you're like, man, if they buy orange juice with pulp in it, that is--

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: I can't live like that. All I'm asking is, if you've ever been in a situation like that, in a relationship where you felt trapped, like you couldn't get out of it, and it was just easier to stay in it, all I'm asking is, even for the briefest of seconds, have you ever accidentally caught yourself thinking how much easier life would be--

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: --if they were to just die?

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: And not because you want them to die, but just because them dying is the easiest way for you to get out of that relationship. And it doesn't involve either one of you getting hurt--

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Daniel Sloss
segments.text: --emotionally.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I have to say, I totally had that thought in my 2018 relationship. And it's not even that you want the other person to die so much as you just kind of want them to evaporate because breaking up with them just feels impossible. I had never said this thought out loud before watching the special. I didn't even know this was a thought other people had.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: And hearing it laid out in such a bare way, I know it would have been impossible to ignore. That's the thing about the show. The jigsaw analogy is a sound that only people in quietly unhappy relationships can hear. If what Daniel is saying reaches you, it's because there's a little radio tower in your head tuned to receive his message.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Aviva DeKornfeld is a producer on our show. Daniel Sloss's specials, including the one you just heard about, are at danielsloss.com/streaming. Watch it if you dare. Coming up, let's do this one Jeopardy-style. The answer is combine "no more tears" baby shampoo and Vaseline into a paste. The question? That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm David Kestenbaum in for Ira Glass. Our show today, You've Come to the Right Person, stories about people finding very specific guides through life's great mysteries. We've arrived at Act Two, "Ask Kwaneta."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So this story is about someone with very specialized knowledge, giving advice in a very specific place. I'll just note, if you're listening with kids, this story includes some adult topics. It's an essay by Kwaneta Harris. And to introduce it, one of our co-workers here, Diane Wu, called her up.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: So, Kwaneta, can you say where you are right now?

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: I am in my cell in Texas in a women's prison.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: And before you were incarcerated, what was your job? What was your special expertise?

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Oh, I was a nurse. I was a nurse who floated from the emergency room to oncology to geriatric care, home health care. Can you hear me OK here? Or should I stand somewhere else? Am I OK?

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Yeah. Where is that? Where are you standing?

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: On top of the toilet seat.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Really? [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Holding my tablet in the air like Lady Liberty.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Like the Statue of Liberty? [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Yeah. And I have the other hand on the wall to hold on.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: So you and I have been working on this story for a while now, right?

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Yes. It's been a minute.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Yeah. And we were hoping to come to the prison and record you, but they denied our request. And since the phone line is bad, and we don't want you to have to read the story standing on top of your toilet, we decided to bring in an actor to read the essay instead.

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Oh, thank god.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Could you read the first couple of lines of the story to get us started? And then we'll cross-fade to the actor.

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: The first thing that happened was I lost everything. I remember exactly the moment I realized it.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I remember exactly the moment I realized it.

segments.speaker: Kwaneta Harris
segments.text: It was in 2009--

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: It was in 2009, just a couple of weeks after I had been transferred from the county jail to prison. I'd injured my shoulder working in the kitchen, stirring pots with canoe-sized paddles.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: So I went to medical. I entered a crowded waiting room, interrupting a lecture by a med tech and a guard, when they asked me, what did I want? With all eyes on me, I said, I need some ibuprofen for my shoulder. The med tech launched into a sermon-- stop looking for a quick fix; stop popping pills; try to stay clean; pray on it; drink more water and lose weight. All that for a few Motrin.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: As she talked, I noticed she was wearing the exact same scrubs I had in my bedroom closet at home-- light blue ones with the pink breast cancer awareness ribbon all over them. It hit me like a body punch to see her in those scrubs, talking to me in such dehumanizing language. Before, she would have been one of my colleagues. Now, I was on this other side, and there was no way back.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: But then, a window back to my old life appeared. I started to get medical questions from the women incarcerated with me. It took a few years. Word got out early on that I was a nurse. But there are many nurses in prison. Some of them are in prison because they were doing nefarious things as a nurse, so people didn't want to ask them for help.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: But once it was cleared up that I wasn't one of the nurses that hurt their patients, I slowly started getting questions. People would come and talk to me in the yard or in the shower. Or when people were too ashamed to ask out loud, they would write it down on a tiny slip of paper and get it to me. First, it was just the girls in my dorm. Then they started asking for their friends, who told their friends.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Now, over a decade later, I get notes from almost every women's prison in Texas. These notes are surreptitiously passed during meal time or laundry exchange, tucked into dirty socks or folded under a tray, passed between women from different prisons on the bus to the prison hospital. Many are from strangers who have just heard that they can write to Mama Detroit-- that's me.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: They're folded up in a square with tiny writing on white or colored pieces of paper, on the inside of candy wrappers, the thin plastic from Kotex pads. I even get questions on squares of toilet paper. One reads, "My roommate uses her inhaler all the time. I think she's addicted to it. Is that possible?"

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Another girl who's in a church choir here wrote about someone she sings with. "When she sings, her breath smells up the whole choir. Her teeth are all rotten, and peppermints are not helping. What can we do?" The range of questions people ask is very wide, anything from, "What's this medicine for?" to, "Which homemade dildo is safest?" None of them.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Everyone involved in passing the notes is taking a risk-- the writer, the person delivering the note, me. If you're caught with a note on you, it can be a disciplinary infraction, possession of contraband. If you have three or more of these infractions in 30 days, that can get upgraded to a major case, which can be used to justify a parole denial. I deliberately store all my unread notes in a brown paper bag in the corner of my cell, so I can always claim it's trash.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Lou wrote to me about her friend Prissy, who bought contraband eyeshadow from someone working in the prison print shop. The print shop has pretty bright-powdered ink that people steal for makeup. Lou wrote that Prissy couldn't get the blue eyeshadow off. "She tried toothpaste. It stained. She looking like a fat-ass Smurf."

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I wrote back, "Mix No More Tears Baby Shampoo and Vaseline into a paste. Apply to your eyelid overnight, then wipe rubbing alcohol repeatedly to the area. It will slowly fade to green and then eventually disappear." I know this won't be the last time someone accidentally cosplays a cartoon character, though. We all miss feeling human, you know? Like our old selves.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: For me, answering these questions, it made me feel like my old self. It was a way for me to still be a caregiver. I felt needed. I was needed in a very particular way I hadn't been on the outside. Because first, the medical care that exists in our prison is extremely lacking. There are only a handful of medical providers for the 1,200 people here. You have to pay to go to medical, $13.55 per visit, which is a king's ransom when we're forced to work in here for free. And when you get there, they treat you like crap.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: And the medical staff can't answer their questions as well as I can because unlike the people they're treating, they aren't incarcerated. I know the materials available to women-- Vaseline, baby shampoo. I know the exact way to ask for certain treatments without getting punished.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Like for yeast infections, going in and saying "I have a yeast infection" will often lead the nurse to start asking about your sex life. And if you let slip that you have a girlfriend, the guards supervising your appointment can write you a disciplinary. The safer way I tell people is to tell the nurse you took antibiotics recently and are noticing this side effect. You have to let the nurse think she figured it out.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Also, I know the various factors the women are weighing when they consider their own care. For instance, early on, one of the most common medical questions people would write to me was, "Do I really need to get a mammogram?"

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I know what they mean when they ask this. We all hate the mammogram trip. We have to take a nausea inducing bus ride that freezes us during the winter and cooks us in the summers. We have to pack all of our belongings to send to storage while we're gone. And when we move back, they assign us a new roommate. It's so hard to get a decent roommate. Few people want to risk losing that by leaving.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: When people ask me if it's worth going on the trip, I write back, explaining breast cancer and ask if their mom or anyone else in their family has a history of cancer. I try to convince them and myself that it's only once a year and probably worth going.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: But the prison instituted a new rule last summer. They now promise to hold our assigned bed and roommate for a week. People are still refusing to go, though, even though you could get a disciplinary infraction if you skipped the trip. Ain't nobody riding in that wheeled cauldron.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: More questions I've received-- "My roommate got lupus. Can I catch it from her?" No, you don't have to worry about that. It's an autoimmune disease, which means it's her body fighting her body. This girl wrote me and said, "I pee only a little bit each time I go. Is this my prostate?" That's not your prostate. You don't have one. This is a UTI.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I have two girls in here who wrote me with signs and symptoms of endometriosis. The problem is, the only way you can diagnose endometriosis is surgery. I'm still figuring out what to write back to them.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I used to think my special expertise was to help women who were incarcerated with me. But then, I started getting mail from released friends, too, like one from my friend I'll call Flaca, who asked me what can she drink to get rid of her pregnancy? She was sexually assaulted by a guest at the motel where she works.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Abortions are illegal in Texas. Flaca has a snitch on her ankle in the form of an electronic GPS monitor, so she can't slip over to New Mexico and get abortion care. She can't get medical abortion pills mailed to her in the faith-based halfway house that opens all incoming mail. Flaca still has to figure out how to get health care while being surveilled and restricted. These days, it feels like women all over Texas do, not just those of us in prison.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: All I could tell her was to call the National Planned Parenthood hotline, not from her phone, because parole officers might search her phone history. I was relieved to hear that she ended up getting the pills by having them delivered to someone else's address. I just hope it's a friend, somebody who won't try to extort or tell on her. Flaca is still on parole. Since receiving Flaca's letter a year ago, I have received eight more letters from women asking for abortion care resources.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: When I've needed medical advice, I don't have anyone to ask for help. I've had to figure out how to be my own Mama Detroit. About nine years ago, I was sent to solitary confinement, and a few years in, I started to feel like I was losing it. I couldn't sleep, and I started to get incredibly emotional.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: One day, one of the girls below me told three of us through a shared heating vent-- that's our phone-- about a letter from her father asking for forgiveness. As I stood listening at my vent, I just couldn't stop crying. This was not normal for me, but I had read about how, in solitary, people react differently to extreme isolation.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Then my memory started to go. I started needing to use my cell walls as a whiteboard to jot down reminders for myself-- the date of my daughter's next volleyball game or what three things I wanted to talk about at my next doctor appointment. My memory has always been really, really good. My second husband used to say that we got divorced because of my memory because I just couldn't let things go. It was hard to let go that he kept cheating.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: So when I started not being able to remember anything, it was a really scary moment for me. I couldn't focus on what I was reading. My body ached. It was late 2020, and I thought, this is long COVID. This is solitary confinement.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: Finally, one of my friends on the outside wrote to me saying, you think it might be menopause? I told her, I am not that old. I was only 48. They never taught us about menopause in nursing school. It was just some punchline about hot flashes, which I started to get, too.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: There isn't air conditioning in our prison building in Texas. It gets so hot in the summer that Coke cans will just spontaneously explode. Toothpaste liquefies. In June 2019, I fainted from the heat, and the sergeant took the temperature in my cell that day-- 129 degrees. So I already felt like I was being cooked before the hot flashes.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: But when that burning feeling hits the middle of my chest, then radiates to the rest of my body, it's unbearable. I learned to keep bowls filled with tap water to dump over my head at the start of each hot flash. I always expect the water to sizzle. So I wrote to my friends back home and asked what they use to treat their menopausal symptoms.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: They told me about black cohosh, flaxseed, apricots, and berries, but the general consensus was that the most effective treatment was estrogen vaginal cream and hormone replacement therapy. My friends inside prison told me, there's no way you're going to get any of those.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I went to dreaded medical and tried for three years to get hormone replacement therapy. I finally got a prescription, and the change was instantaneous. It was like a switch turned me back into the old me. My skin cleared up, my hair regained thickness, my mood was lighter, and the brain fog cleared. Best of all, the hot flashes stopped. It was a miracle drug, until the prescription ran out after two months. The doctors would not give me a refill. That was two years ago.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: So here I am, living with all my symptoms, waiting for this phase to pass. The symptoms can last a decade. Studies show Black women experience more hot flashes, longer hot flashes, and longer perimenopause. I learned this from the radio and from a pamphlet about menopause that I asked my lawyer to send me.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: When I tried to learn more by ordering books like The Menopause Manifesto, the prison denied the books for being sexually explicit. Meanwhile, I've gotten a few questions from other neighbors about menopause. We're all getting older in here.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: After all these years, I'm not tired of answering questions yet, but I am tired of answering the same questions. I am tired of repeating the same answers. Depo shot is the name of the birth control everyone wants because the guards don't hand out enough pads and tampons. The flu shot will not give you the flu. No, the COVID vaccine didn't have a chip in it. Tampons don't cause cancer. They don't cause infertility.

segments.speaker: Kecia Lewis
segments.text: I thought by 2025, we'd move on to something else. But the girls still aren't getting this information anywhere else. I wish I could put the 10 most asked questions on a flyer and just pass them out. But that's not how it works in here. So I keep writing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Kwaneta Harris's story was read by the actor Kecia Lewis. You can see her on Broadway now, in her Tony Award-winning role in the musical, Hell's Kitchen.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: We did reach out to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice for comment. They told us that guards are not supposed to be writing disciplinary infractions for notes, unless they are violent or drug-related, and that The Menopause Manifesto is on the approved book list. Also, Kwaneta has moved prisons over the years. In her current one, the mammogram trip isn't as long.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Our story was produced by Diane Wu. You can find more of Kwaneta's writing on her Substack, Write or Die, Raw Dispatches from a Texas Women's Prison.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Act Three, "Ask Harriotte." So earlier in the show, we had a story about how to know when to leave a relationship. This last story is about a woman who wishes she had that problem. And for the second time in today's show, here's Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna's life outside of dating is as busy as a rom-com heroine's. She lives outside Boston, near her family and a ton of beloved friends. She has a job she likes, fills her free time with jujitsu and weightlifting. She can deadlift 370 pounds, which, if you don't know what that means, it's as impressive as it sounds. Juna's dream is to meet someone at the gym, but that hasn't happened yet.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Because a lot of men are very afraid to approach women at the gym, which I totally understand because, obviously, people, a lot of time, don't want to be disturbed in their workouts.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: But there are people that want to be disturbed-- me-- by a hot man. Anyways.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna is 29 and has never had a boyfriend-- not for lack of trying. In high school and college, she was a nerdy pianist who didn't really date. But five years ago, she got on the apps. On her first date, she was so nervous that her teeth were chattering as she waited for the guy to arrive. It didn't go great. Very few of them have. Sometimes, it feels like in her friend group, she's the last one standing.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: I feel like we've always all been single, like a lot of my best friends. And now they're all in relationships. And that's when I'm like, it's because I'm blind.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna's been blind since she was a little kid. She grew up in Albania, moved to Boston when she was five. The way her blindness works is that everything is very, very blurry. She reads on her phone by zooming in a lot and then holding it right up to her face. The friends she's thinking of who've paired off, they're sighted.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: There's no other thing that explains why it's been so difficult for me. I just, like, can't pinpoint another thing that separates me from the other people that I feel like are successful besides being blind.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna's like, I think I'm at least average pretty. I think she's pretty. I'm fun to talk to-- also true. What gives? She experiments with putting that she's blind on her dating profile. The number of matches she gets plummets-- it doesn't surprise her. She feels like meeting people in real life is also harder because of things like eye contact, which doesn't come naturally to her.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: I will often look at people's mouths because that's what their voice comes from. So I think I'm always, like, 4 inches under eye contact. And sometimes I'll consciously make an effort to look higher than where I want to look. But then I get very uncomfortable because another big insecurity I have is that my eyes make people uncomfortable. And so I kind of feel bad looking at them in the eye. So basically, I've just given up on looking at people's eyes. I'll just look at their mouth.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna was sort of resigned to having a bad time of it. But then a couple of years ago, her friend's mom told her, my friend Harriotte is blind, too. You guys should meet. Juna was pretty skeptical at first, but liked Harriotte right away. They're both musicians, both very talkative.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: But what really stood out to Juna was Harriotte's bountiful love life. She's 78 and has had three husbands and more boyfriends than she can count-- even an affair, which seemed to really impress Juna. Juna has always wanted to ask her, what's your secret? What should I be doing differently? We went over to Harriotte's home one December evening to find out. Her partner, Frank, let us in.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Hi, Frank.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: In the kitchen, Juna tells me one of her favorite stories, the story of how Harriotte and Frank met 20 years ago.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Harriotte and Frank met on a red line train. Harriotte was playing recorder, and Frank heard it and was like, can you teach me that song? Right, guys?

segments.speaker: Frank
segments.text: Yeah, that's how it happened.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: He sat down next to me, and he said, I have my recorder with me.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Which is crazy. Like, Frank, why did you have your recorder with you?

segments.speaker: Frank
segments.text: I don't know. That was a certain time in my life.

segments.speaker: Frank
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: They played together on the train, exchanged numbers, became friends, and five years into that friendship, started dating. We sit around the kitchen table and get down to business.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: OK. Shall we begin?

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: So, Harriotte--

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Yes, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna starts by explaining how her dating life has gone so far-- no real success, her conclusion that blindness is getting in her way.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: So in your idea of your life, right, if you think back on your life, have you ever thought to yourself that your vision impacts your dating? Or has it, to you, just not been a related topic?

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Not been a related topic except to share with people all the amazing experiences that I have kinesthetically and otherwise as a blind person.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Let's say like meeting people in person, right? One thing that I feel like is very difficult is that I can't make eye contact. And I--

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: I never could, baby. So I don't know what you're talking about.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: [LAUGHS] But Harriotte, all, like, the videos on TikTok about how to meet people at the gym and stuff or whatever, is like, the person makes eye contact with you, and then you smile to let them know that you're available to come-- Harriotte's waving her hands. Harriotte, why-- [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: No, I just bump into them awkwardly and say, where's the treadmill?

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Oh, yeah. OK, I do that, too, sometimes, but like--

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: No, but I mean, with panache, you know? With ease, you know? Like, hey, where's the bathroom? Can you walk me over there? Thank you. I'll get it fixed. I'll do it better next time, you know? Whatever. But don't you see? It's like, we're unwilling to be vulnerable. Everybody is.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Well, not Harriotte.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: I have no problem. I'll stand up in the subway and say, hey, anybody getting off at X spot? I have to cross over from the A line to the West 4th Street, whatever.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: That's crazy! I have literally been lost for hours because I refused to ask for help. I'm like, I'm going to wander around until I find where to go to avoid asking for help. So-- now Harriotte's laughing at me.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: No, not at you. I'm just laughing at the discomfort and awfulness of it, you know?

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Juna's default mode is to be completely competent in everything she does. She hates being underestimated or condescended to. This is her way of protecting herself from all of that. But talking to Harriotte, she realizes it might come with a downside. Like when Juna's friend invites her to go salsa dancing, even though she wants to try it, she doesn't. She worries the way she dances might look embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Do you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Do you realize how much you're basing all of your perceptions, at least from where I'm sitting with this, on the sighted world?

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: But the sighted world is the world, Harriotte. Like--

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: It is, but it hasn't been a problem. I still feel that my world has total integrity.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: I feel like my world has total integrity, too, but I feel like-- I don't know.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: I think the hardest thing in life, whether you're sighted or anything, is a deeper self-acceptance, really. And that doesn't matter what the hell other people react to or what they think or whatever.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Whatever you're sensing from me, do you think that that plays a role into why it might be hard for me to date people?

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: OK, why?

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Because you have a lens, you have a filter that is constantly on high that says they're not going to get me. They're going to put me down. They're going to ignore me. They're going to pity me. And if that is sort of in the emotional undercurrent within you, then it'll amplify everything--

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Except yourself. It's hard to know what to do with that kind of advice.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: What do you think that I should do differently? But you can't say you have to deeply accept yourself because I just don't even know what that means. So it's like--

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: OK, that's fine.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Harriotte gives her a concrete thing to try. Juna's been taking jiu-jitsu classes that she really loves with mostly guys, and she has a crush on one of them.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Just see if they want to go out and have coffee or tea.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: I just don't think people do that anymore, Harriotte.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: What? So what? Maybe they're all waiting.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: I don't want to be the one to do it. Why can't they do it?

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: I always make the first move.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: But Harriotte!

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: Treat it as friendship. It's just a thought.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: No, I think you're right. Like, the guy I have a crush on, for example, me and my friends call him my husband.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Like, my friend was like, your husband is not in class today. And I'm like, how am I supposed to go talk to my husband? I'm too scared. I'm scared.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: No, no, no, you have to reset. Reset.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: So last week, Harriotte, I was in class, and my jiu-jitsu husband usually will ask me to spar once in class. And this time, we only had one spar. Long story short, we didn't get to spar. And I'd only come to class to see my jiu-jitsu husband.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: And so I saw him on the mat, right? And I was like, I'll go ask him. But I was scared. But I was like, I'll go ask him because he always asks me. I'll go ask him. And I went to go ask him. And he's like a very shy, introverted person. And I asked him. He's like, oh, um, yeah. Actually, I was stretching because I was going to leave, but yeah, I guess we can spar. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: And I was like, oh, no, it's OK. We can do it next time. Yeah, OK. And I ran back to the lockers, and he came up to me. He was like, no, no, no, let's do it. And I was like, no, no, no, it's OK. We can do it another time. He was like, no, let's spar.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: Anyways, it took him, like, three different times to be like, no, let's do it, let's do it, let's do it. And then we did. And I was like, I'm never talking to him again. Like, he can talk to me if he wants, but I am never speaking to him again in class because I was so embarrassed.

segments.speaker: Harriotte
segments.text: The fact that he asked you the three times is already not saying I want to be your husband, but it is saying, I would like to do that. So it's authentic. I think he's asking from, just my sense about it, from a very authentic place. And so build on it. Just get to know him. When you finish sparring, you could say, if you would like to go to brunch sometime, just the two of us after jiu-jitsu, let me know.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: [SIGHS] OK.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: So it's been three weeks since you went and talked to Harriotte, and I'm calling to see, are there any updates?

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Oh, my god, I feel like I'm on one of those dating shows. Anyways, so I went the first time after talking to Harriotte, and I was like, you know what? Let me treat this person the same way I treat everybody else in this class and just be normal and be his friend. And so I started talking to him, and it was like the worst conversation I've ever had in my entire life, not because of me. It was like talking to a brick wall, you guys. It was like--

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Juna
segments.text: --so terrible. And I went to the dog park the next day, and I was like, you guys, I think he has literally no personality. And they were like, then why do you like him? And I said, I literally think it's just because of his arms. And I have been so stupid. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A very wise person once tweeted, "A crush is just a lack of information," though, for Juna, getting that information-- progress. Juna, determined to follow Harriotte's instructions, actually continued befriending the guy, who ended up being much more fun to talk to later. She still seems a long way from ever making the first move, but now, at least, she knows it's an option.
